opus-5.5.text:
I think it's useful to distinguish between evolutionary algorithms in the classical sense and what I'd call a broader evolutionary or open-ended approach. Classical evolutionary algorithms, genetic algorithms, evolution strategies and so on, are really optimization methods. You have a population, a fitness function, mutation and selection, and you're trying to push towards some fixed objective. That's been around for decades and it works well in certain settings, but it's not fundamentally different from other black-box optimizers.

What gets me excited is something a bit different. If you look at biological evolution, or at human culture and science, the interesting thing isn't that it optimizes a single objective. It's that it keeps producing novel, interesting artifacts, and each one becomes a stepping stone for the next. That's the open-endedness perspective, and people like Ken Stanley, Joel Lehman and Jeff Clune have been arguing for it for a long time. The problem historically was that we didn't have good mutation operators, and we didn't have a good way of judging what counts as "interesting."

Foundation models change both sides of that. On the variation side, a large language model is an incredibly powerful mutation operator. Instead of randomly flipping bits or perturbing parameters, you can ask the model to take an existing program, a prompt, an environment or a research idea and propose a meaningful variation. It has absorbed a huge amount of human knowledge about what sensible changes look like, so the search becomes much more directed. We explored this with Promptbreeder, where the model evolves not only task prompts but also the mutation prompts themselves, so the variation process improves over time. You see similar ideas in work like FunSearch and in systems that evolve code or agents.

On the selection side, foundation models also encode a notion of what humans find interesting or novel. You can use them as a proxy for interestingness, which was always the hardest part of open-ended search. You can't hand-write a fitness function for "surprising and worthwhile," but a model trained on human data has a reasonable sense of it.

So the relationship, as I see it, is that the evolutionary algorithm provides the outer loop: keep an archive, generate variations, select, iterate. Foundation models plug into that loop as both the generator and the evaluator. You get the benefits of population-based, quality-diversity style search, but with operators far more capable than anything we had before.

And I'd argue this matters beyond being a neat technique. If we want systems that keep improving and discovering things we haven't seen, rather than plateauing once they've absorbed human data, we need open-ended processes on top of these models. Foundation models alone are trained to imitate the existing distribution. Wrapping them in an evolutionary, open-ended loop is one of the most promising ways I know of to move beyond that distribution and generate genuinely new knowledge.

r001.rationale: The response describes foundation models supplying the generator and evaluator roles in an established evolutionary search loop, replacing or upgrading components of that method.

r002.rationale: It explicitly calls a large language model a powerful mutation operator that proposes meaningful variations to existing candidates.

r003.rationale: It says foundation models can serve as evaluators and proxies for interestingness in the selection loop, communicating that they judge candidates' interestingness.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I think the way I'd frame it is that evolutionary algorithms, in the classical sense, are really a search procedure. You have a population of candidate solutions, you apply some kind of variation operator, mutation or crossover, you evaluate fitness, you select, and you iterate. And historically the bottleneck has always been the variation operator. Random mutations in some genotype space are incredibly inefficient, because most mutations are either neutral or destructive, and you need enormous populations and enormous compute to find anything interesting.

What foundation models change is that they give you a variation operator that's actually intelligent. If you ask a language model to take a piece of code, or a prompt, or an environment description, and propose a modification, it doesn't propose random edits. It proposes edits that are plausible given everything it's absorbed from human-generated data. So you're essentially replacing random mutation with mutation that's informed by a prior over what good solutions tend to look like. That's a very different regime. The search becomes dramatically more sample efficient, and you can operate in spaces, like natural language or source code, where it was never obvious how to define a sensible mutation operator in the first place.

But I'd say the relationship goes both ways, and that's the part I find most exciting. Foundation models on their own are quite limited in a specific way: they're good at interpolating within the distribution of their training data, but they don't have a built-in mechanism for going beyond it. Evolutionary and open-ended processes supply exactly that. They give you selection pressure, they give you the ability to accumulate improvements over many generations, and they give you the capacity to discover things that no single forward pass of the model would have produced. So you get this loop where the model proposes, the environment or the evaluation selects, and the artifacts that survive feed back and change what gets proposed next.

That's why I think of this less as "evolutionary algorithms using LLMs as a tool" and more as the beginning of a genuinely open-ended approach to AI. The classical evolutionary algorithm literature was always interested in open-endedness, in processes that keep generating novelty indefinitely rather than converging to a single optimum. It just never had a generator powerful enough to sustain it. Foundation models might be that generator. And if that's right, then the interesting question isn't how to use evolution to tune models, it's how to build systems where the model and the evolutionary process together keep producing things that are new and learnable, without a human having to specify the objective in advance.

r001.rationale: The response describes replacing random mutation with a foundation-model-guided variation operator in evolutionary algorithms, but does not identify a broader trend of replacing components across established AI methods.

r002.rationale: It explicitly describes a language model proposing plausible modifications in place of random mutation within an evolutionary search loop.

r003.rationale: Selection is described as performed by the environment or evaluation process; the response does not say the language model judges which candidate example is more interesting.

astra-6.text:
I think evolutionary algorithms are one concrete instance of a broader idea: instead of specifying a solution directly, you create a process that can discover solutions through variation and selection. With foundation models, we now have a very different way of generating that variation. Rather than making random changes to a candidate, you can use a model to propose changes that are informed by what it has learned.

For example, if you’re evolving programs, a model can suggest a meaningful modification to an existing program. You can then execute it, evaluate it, and use that feedback to decide which candidates to build on. So you have this combination of a learned prior over promising solutions and an evolutionary search process that tests whether those solutions actually work.

But I’d distinguish that from open-endedness. An evolutionary algorithm can optimize a fixed objective and eventually converge. The broader ambition is to build systems that keep generating new challenges and new capabilities, where the space of interesting outcomes isn’t completely specified beforehand. Foundation models could be powerful components of those systems, but you still need mechanisms for evaluation, maintaining diversity, and producing challenges that drive further progress.

r001.rationale: It describes replacing random variation in evolutionary algorithms with foundation-model-proposed changes, identifying a foundation model as a substitute for an established method component.

r002.rationale: It says a model can propose meaningful modifications to an existing program, which are evaluated and used to build on candidates—describing the model as a mutation operator.

r003.rationale: It describes evaluating candidates for whether they work, but does not say a language model judges which candidate is more interesting than another.

sol-6.1.text:
I think evolutionary algorithms are one concrete way of implementing a much broader idea: rather than trying to design the solution directly, you design a process that can discover solutions. You have variation, some mechanism for evaluating what gets produced, and selection. And then you repeat that process.

With foundation models, what’s interesting is that we now have a very powerful source of variation. Instead of randomly perturbing a program and hoping it still does something useful, you can ask a model to propose a meaningful modification. That doesn’t guarantee improvement, but it changes what you can explore. You can put that inside a loop where you execute the program, evaluate it, and use the results to guide the next set of proposals.

So I wouldn’t equate the broader evolutionary approach with a particular evolutionary algorithm. It’s more about how you organize discovery around these models. The model brings knowledge acquired during training, and the outer loop lets you search, test, and accumulate improvements. A lot then depends on the environment and the feedback: what are you selecting for, and does that actually capture the thing you care about?

r001.rationale: The response describes foundation models as a source of variation in a discovery process, but does not identify a broader trend of replacing components of established AI methods with foundation models.

r002.rationale: It describes asking a model to propose meaningful program modifications as variation within a loop that executes, evaluates, and iterates on candidates.

r003.rationale: It mentions evaluating and selecting candidates, but does not say that the language model judges whether one candidate is more interesting than another.
